title: Errors, Files and the Standard Library

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.summary: Handle errors with try/except/else/finally, raise your own exceptions and build custom ones.
topics.description:
Errors at runtime are raised as **exceptions**. Unhandled, they stop the program with a traceback. Handling them lets your program recover or fail gracefully.

### The full structure
```python
try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError as e:
    print("not a number:", e)
except (TypeError, KeyError):
    ...
else:
    print("ran only if no exception")
finally:
    print("always runs (cleanup)")
```

### Raising
`raise ValueError("bad input")`. Inside an `except` block a bare `raise` re-raises the same error. `raise NewError(...) from original` keeps the cause chained, which is very useful in logs.

### Custom exceptions
Subclass `Exception` to express domain problems clearly, and give related errors a common base:
```python
class AppError(Exception): ...
class NotFound(AppError): ...
```

### Hierarchy
`BaseException` -> `Exception` -> `ValueError`, `TypeError`, `KeyError`, `OSError` (with `FileNotFoundError`), `ZeroDivisionError`, etc. Catch the **most specific** exception you can handle.

### EAFP vs LBYL
Python style prefers **EAFP** ("easier to ask forgiveness than permission"): try the operation and catch failures, rather than checking everything first.

### Python 3.11+
`ExceptionGroup` and `except*` handle multiple errors raised together (used by `asyncio.TaskGroup`). `add_note()` attaches extra info.
keyPoints: Catch specific exceptions, not bare except:
else runs when no error; finally always runs
raise ... from ... preserves the cause
Custom exceptions should subclass Exception
Prefer EAFP: try first, handle failure
pitfalls: Bare except: that hides bugs and swallows KeyboardInterrupt
Catching Exception and doing nothing
Using exceptions for normal control flow in hot loops

examples.title: try/except/else/finally

interview.q: What is the difference between else and finally?
interview.a: else runs only when the try block raised nothing; finally runs always, whether or not an exception occurred, and is used for cleanup.
It catches everything including SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt and hides real bugs. Catch specific exceptions.

topics.title: Files and pathlib
topics.summary: Read and write text and binary files safely and build OS-independent paths with pathlib.
topics.description:
### Reading and writing
Always use `with` so the file is closed automatically, and always give an encoding for text:

```python
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:            # lazy, memory friendly
        print(line.rstrip())
```

### Modes
`r` read (default), `w` write (truncates), `a` append, `x` create-only, `b` binary (`rb`, `wb`), `+` read and write.

### Reading methods
`f.read()` whole file, `f.readline()` one line, `f.readlines()` a list of lines, and iterating `for line in f` which is the best for big files.

### pathlib
`pathlib.Path` represents file-system paths as objects and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

```python
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("data") / "users.csv"
p.exists(); p.suffix; p.stem; p.parent; p.name
p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
p.write_text("abc", encoding="utf-8")
p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for f in Path(".").glob("*.py"): ...
```

### Other helpers
`shutil` for copy/move/delete trees, `tempfile` for temporary files, `os.environ` for environment variables.

Never build paths with string concatenation or hard-coded backslashes; use `/` with `Path`.

### Practical advice
Paths in a script are relative to the **current working directory**, which is not always the script's folder. When you need files next to your script, anchor on `Path(__file__).parent`. For large files never call `read()`; iterate lines or read in chunks. When you write data that must not be half-written (config, state), write to a temporary file and then rename it, because a rename is atomic on most systems. Binary files such as images or PDFs use the `"rb"` and `"wb"` modes and return `bytes` instead of `str`.
keyPoints: Use with open(...) so files close automatically
Specify encoding="utf-8" for text files
Iterate a file object line by line for large files
pathlib.Path with the / operator builds portable paths
Path.read_text and write_text cover small files
pitfalls: Opening with "w" and accidentally truncating an existing file
Forgetting the encoding on Windows
Concatenating paths with + and hard-coded separators

examples.title: Path operations (no disk access)
examples.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath

p = PurePosixPath("projects") / "site" / "report.final.csv"
print(p)
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.parent)
print(p.with_suffix(".json"))
print(p.parts)
print(p.is_absolute())
examples.explanation: PurePath objects work without touching the disk, so they are safe to run here.

examples.title: Real file read/write
examples.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("output")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

target = folder / "log.txt"
with target.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("run started\n")

for number, line in enumerate(target.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
    print(number, line)

for csv_file in Path(".").rglob("*.csv"):
    print(csv_file, csv_file.stat().st_size)

interview.a: The context manager guarantees the file is closed even if an exception occurs, preventing leaks and unflushed data.
It offers an object-oriented, readable API, portable path joining with /, and convenient methods like read_text, glob and mkdir.

topics.title: Modules, Packages and Imports
topics.summary: Split code into files and folders, import it cleanly and understand __name__ == "__main__".
topics.description:
A **module** is any `.py` file. A **package** is a folder of modules (traditionally with an `__init__.py`). Modules let you organise code, avoid name clashes and reuse functionality.

### Import styles
```python
import math
from math import sqrt, pi
import numpy as np
from package.module import func as f
```
Avoid `from x import *`; it pollutes the namespace and hides where names come from.

### Import search path
Python looks in the script's directory, then `PYTHONPATH`, then the standard library and `site-packages`. Inspect it with `sys.path`. Imported modules are cached in `sys.modules`, so a module body runs only once.

### Project layout
```text
myapp/
  main.py
  utils.py
  services/
    __init__.py
    email.py
```
Use `from services.email import send` or relative imports `from .email import send` inside a package.

### The main guard
```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
`__name__` is `"__main__"` when the file is run directly and the module name when it is imported, so test code and CLI entry points don't run on import.

### Circular imports
If module A imports B and B imports A, you may get partially initialised modules. Fix by restructuring, moving the import inside a function, or extracting shared code.

### Standard library highlights
`os`, `sys`, `pathlib`, `json`, `re`, `datetime`, `collections`, `itertools`, `random`, `math`, `argparse`, `subprocess`.
keyPoints: A module is a file; a package is a folder of modules
Use explicit imports; avoid import *
if __name__ == "__main__" separates script from import use
Modules are cached in sys.modules and run once
Break circular imports by restructuring
pitfalls: Naming your file like a standard module (random.py, json.py)
Circular imports
Relying on the current working directory instead of package structure

examples.title: Project with a package

interview.a: It runs the code only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported as a module.
It marks a directory as a regular package and can contain package-level initialisation or re-exports. Namespace packages work without it.

topics.title: JSON and CSV
topics.summary: Convert between Python objects and JSON text, and read or write tabular CSV data.
topics.description:
### JSON
JSON is the standard data format of web APIs. The `json` module maps JSON to Python types: object -> `dict`, array -> `list`, string -> `str`, number -> `int`/`float`, true/false -> `True`/`False`, null -> `None`.

- `json.loads(text)` string -> object, `json.dumps(obj, indent=2)` object -> string.
- `json.load(f)` and `json.dump(obj, f)` work with file objects.
- Options: `indent`, `sort_keys=True`, `ensure_ascii=False`, `default=str` for unsupported types such as `datetime`.

JSON only has string keys, so `{1: "a"}` comes back as `{"1": "a"}`. Tuples become arrays and sets cannot be serialised without conversion.

### CSV
`csv` handles quoting and delimiters correctly, so never split lines by commas yourself.

- `csv.reader` gives lists; `csv.DictReader` gives dicts keyed by header.
- `csv.writer` / `csv.DictWriter` for output. Open files with `newline=""` and an explicit encoding.

```python
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "age"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({"name": "Asha", "age": 25})
```

### When to use what
JSON for nested data and APIs; CSV for flat tables and spreadsheets; `pandas.read_csv` once the data is large or needs analysis.
keyPoints: json.loads/dumps work on strings; load/dump on files
JSON keys are always strings
Use DictReader/DictWriter for header-based CSV
Open CSV files with newline="" and an encoding
default= handles non-serialisable types
pitfalls: Splitting CSV lines manually on commas
Forgetting that CSV values are all strings
Trying to dump datetime or set without a converter

examples.title: JSON and CSV with in-memory data
examples.code:
import csv
import io
import json

data = {"name": "Asha", "skills": ["python", "sql"], "active": True, "boss": None}
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["skills"][0], back == data)

raw = "name,age\nAsha,25\nRavi,31\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw)))
print(rows)
print(sum(int(r["age"]) for r in rows))

out = io.StringIO()
w = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=["name", "city"])
w.writeheader()
w.writerow({"name": "Mia", "city": "Rome, Italy"})
print(out.getvalue())

interview.q: How does JSON map to Python types?
interview.a: object->dict, array->list, string->str, number->int/float, true/false->bool, null->None.
It gives each row as a dict using the header, making code readable and independent of column order.

topics.title: Dates and Times
topics.summary: Work with date, time, datetime, timedelta, formatting, parsing and time zones.
topics.description:
The `datetime` module has four main classes:

- `date(2025, 3, 14)` a calendar date.
- `time(10, 30)` a time of day.
- `datetime(2025, 3, 14, 10, 30)` both together.
- `timedelta(days=7, hours=2)` a duration.

### Arithmetic
`datetime - datetime` gives a `timedelta`; `datetime + timedelta` gives a new `datetime`. Use `.total_seconds()`, `.days`.

### Formatting and parsing
- `dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")` object -> string.
- `datetime.strptime("2025-03-14", "%Y-%m-%d")` string -> object.
- `dt.isoformat()` and `datetime.fromisoformat(...)` for ISO 8601, the best interchange format.

Common codes: `%Y` year, `%m` month, `%d` day, `%H` hour, `%M` minute, `%S` second, `%A` weekday name, `%b` month abbreviation.

### Time zones
A **naive** datetime has no timezone; an **aware** one does. Use `zoneinfo` (3.9+):
```python
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata"))
```
Best practice: store and compute in **UTC**, convert to local time only for display.

### Others
`time.time()` is the Unix timestamp; `time.sleep(1)` pauses; `calendar` module gives month layouts; `dateutil` (third party) parses messy date strings.
keyPoints: timedelta represents a duration and supports arithmetic
strftime formats, strptime parses
Use ISO 8601 strings for storage and APIs
Prefer timezone-aware datetimes and store UTC
zoneinfo replaces pytz in modern Python
pitfalls: Mixing naive and aware datetimes (TypeError)
Using datetime.utcnow() which returns a naive object (deprecated)
Hard-coding date formats that differ per locale

examples.title: Date arithmetic and formatting
examples.code:
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone

d = date(2025, 3, 14)
print(d.strftime("%A, %d %B %Y"))
print(d + timedelta(days=30))

start = datetime(2025, 1, 1, 9, 30)
end = datetime(2025, 1, 3, 17, 0)
diff = end - start
print(diff, diff.days, diff.total_seconds() / 3600)

parsed = datetime.strptime("2025-12-25 18:45", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
print(parsed.isoformat())
print(datetime.fromisoformat("2025-12-25T18:45:00") == parsed)

utc = datetime(2025, 6, 1, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(utc.isoformat())
print((date(2025, 12, 31) - date(2025, 1, 1)).days)

interview.q: What is the difference between naive and aware datetimes?
interview.a: A naive datetime carries no timezone information; an aware one has tzinfo, so it represents an exact moment and can be converted safely.

interview.q: How do you get the difference between two dates in days?
interview.a: Subtract them to get a timedelta and read its .days attribute.

topics.title: Regular Expressions
topics.summary: Search, match and extract text patterns with the re module.
topics.description:
Regular expressions describe text patterns. The `re` module provides the engine.

### Main functions
- `re.search(p, s)` first match anywhere (returns a match object or `None`).
- `re.match(p, s)` match only at the start; `re.fullmatch` the whole string.
- `re.findall(p, s)` list of all matches (or groups).
- `re.finditer(p, s)` iterator of match objects.
- `re.sub(p, repl, s)` replace; `re.split(p, s)`.
- `re.compile(p)` precompile a pattern you reuse.

### Pattern cheat sheet
| Token | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `.` | any char except newline |
| `\d \w \s` | digit, word char, space |
| `^ $` | start, end |
| `* + ?` | 0+, 1+, 0 or 1 |
| `{n,m}` | between n and m |
| `[abc]` `[^abc]` | set, negated set |
| `( )` | capture group |
| `(?P<name>...)` | named group |
| `a|b` | alternation |

### Tips
- Use **raw strings** (`r"\d+"`) so backslashes are not escape sequences.
- Quantifiers are greedy; add `?` (`.*?`) for lazy matching.
- Flags: `re.I` ignore case, `re.M` multiline, `re.S` dot matches newline, `re.X` verbose.
- Do not parse HTML with regex; use BeautifulSoup or lxml instead.
keyPoints: Use raw strings for patterns
search finds anywhere, match anchors at the start
Groups ( ) capture; named groups improve readability
.* is greedy, .*? is lazy
Compile patterns you reuse in loops
pitfalls: Forgetting that match() only checks the start
Greedy patterns swallowing too much
Using regex to parse nested HTML or JSON

examples.title: Extracting data
examples.code: import re text = "Contact: asha@example.com, ravi.k@work.org | Phone: 98765-43210 | Date: 2025-03-14" emails = re.findall(r"[\w.]+@[\w.]+\.\w+", text) print(emails) m = re.search(r"(?P\d{4})-(?P\d{2})-(?P\d{2})", text) print(m.group("y"), m.group("m"), m.group("d"), m.groupdict()) print(re.sub(r"\d", "#", "Order 123 and 45")) print(re.split(r"[,;|]\s*", "a, b;c|d")) print(re.findall(r"(.*?)", "one and two")) print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{5}-\d{5}", "98765-43210")))

interview.a: match only matches at the beginning of the string; search scans the string for the first match anywhere.

interview.q: What are greedy and lazy quantifiers?
interview.a: Greedy ones (*, +) match as much as possible; adding ? makes them lazy, matching as little as possible.

topics.title: Logging
topics.summary: Replace print debugging with leveled, configurable logs using the logging module.
topics.description:
`print()` is fine for scripts, but real applications need **logging**: severity levels, timestamps, destinations (console, files, remote services) and the ability to turn detail up or down without changing code.

### Levels (low to high)
`DEBUG` < `INFO` < `WARNING` (default threshold) < `ERROR` < `CRITICAL`.

### Quick setup
```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("started")
log.error("failed", exc_info=True)   # includes traceback
```

### Core concepts
- **Logger**: what you call (`logging.getLogger(__name__)`), arranged in a dotted hierarchy.
- **Handler**: where records go (`StreamHandler`, `FileHandler`, `RotatingFileHandler`).
- **Formatter**: how records look.
- **Filter**: which records pass.

### Best practices
- One logger per module with `__name__`.
- Use lazy formatting: `log.info("user %s logged in", name)`.
- `log.exception("...")` inside `except` logs the traceback at ERROR level.
- Libraries should not configure logging; applications do.
- Never log passwords, tokens or personal data.

Django and Flask both use this same module, so these skills transfer directly.
keyPoints: Levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
Use logging.getLogger(__name__) per module
logging.exception() records the traceback
Handlers decide destination; formatters decide layout
Pass arguments with %s style instead of f-strings
pitfalls: Calling basicConfig in library code
Logging secrets or personal data
Expecting DEBUG messages without lowering the level

examples.title: Logging to stdout
examples.code:
import logging
import sys

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.DEBUG,
    stream=sys.stdout,
    format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger("shop")

log.debug("loading cart")
log.info("user %s added %d items", "asha", 3)
log.warning("stock is low")
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError as err:
    log.error("calculation failed: %s", err)
# log.exception("...") would also print the full traceback

interview.q: Why use logging instead of print?
interview.a: Logging has severity levels, timestamps, multiple destinations and runtime configuration, so you can control output without editing code.

interview.q: What is the default logging level?
interview.a: WARNING: DEBUG and INFO messages are hidden until you configure a lower level.

topics.title: Context Managers and the with Statement
topics.summary: Guarantee setup and cleanup using with, __enter__/__exit__ and contextlib.
topics.description:
A **context manager** wraps a block of code with setup and teardown that always happens, even if an exception is raised. You already use it with files:

```python
with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()
# file is closed here
```

### Where they are used
Files, locks (`with lock:`), database transactions, temporary directories, network connections, changing the working directory, suppressing exceptions, timing blocks.

### Writing one: class based
```python
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        return False   # do not swallow exceptions
```
`__exit__` receives the exception info; returning `True` suppresses the exception.

### Writing one: generator based
`contextlib.contextmanager` is shorter:
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tag(name):
    print(f"<{name}>")
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f"</{name}>")
```

### contextlib extras
`suppress(FileNotFoundError)`, `redirect_stdout`, `closing`, `ExitStack` (manage a dynamic number of contexts), `nullcontext`.

Multiple managers can share a statement: `with open(a) as f, open(b, "w") as g:`.

### Why it matters
Without `with` you must remember `try/finally` everywhere, and forgetting it leaks file handles, leaves locks held forever or keeps database transactions open. A context manager moves that discipline into one reusable object, so each caller just writes `with`. In web code you will see this for database sessions, `requests.Session()`, Selenium or Playwright browsers, and transaction blocks such as Django's `transaction.atomic()`.
keyPoints: with guarantees cleanup even when errors occur
__enter__ sets up; __exit__ tears down
@contextmanager turns a generator into a context manager
Returning True from __exit__ swallows the exception
contextlib.suppress ignores specific exceptions
pitfalls: Forgetting try/finally inside a @contextmanager generator
Accidentally swallowing exceptions by returning True
Using the resource after the with block has closed it

examples.title: Two ways to write one
examples.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager, suppress

class Managed:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("setup")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print("cleanup", exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return False

@contextmanager
def tag(name):
    print(f"<{name}>")
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f"</{name}>")

with Managed():
    print("working")

with tag("section"):
    print("inside")

try:
    with Managed():
        raise ValueError("boom")
except ValueError:
    print("caught outside")

with suppress(KeyError):
    {}["missing"]
print("done")

interview.a: It calls __enter__ on the object before the block and __exit__ after it, even if an exception happens, so cleanup is guaranteed.

interview.q: How can you create a context manager quickly?
interview.a: Use the @contextlib.contextmanager decorator on a generator function with a single yield, wrapping the yield in try/finally.
